findings_initial.title: request_reset() has a fast-path/slow-path timing difference that leaks account existence
findings_initial.requirement: The service's own stated contract (app/auth.py:96, 'Don't reveal whether an account exists') and OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet's requirement that response behavior be indistinguishable for existing vs. non-existing accounts, including timing.
findings_initial.evidence: app/auth.py:94-109 — for an unknown email the method returns immediately after a single dict lookup; for a known email it generates a token, writes to _tokens, formats a link, and calls mailer.send(). No constant-time/dummy-work path exists for the unknown-email branch.
findings_initial.failure: An attacker measuring response latency (especially once Mailer is a real network call, e.g. SMTP/SES) can distinguish registered from unregistered emails and enumerate the user base, exactly the outcome the in-code comment says the implementation is trying to prevent.

findings_initial.title: Requesting a new reset link does not invalidate previously issued, still-valid tokens for the same user
findings_initial.requirement: OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet: 'Old, unused password reset tokens ... expire after a set time or, ideally, after the user makes a new request' — only the most recently issued reset token should be usable.
findings_initial.evidence: app/auth.py:99-101 — request_reset() always mints a fresh token and adds it to self._tokens without looking up or removing any prior (email, expiry) entries already stored for that email.
findings_initial.failure: A user who clicks 'forgot password' twice (or an attacker who triggers repeated reset emails) leaves multiple simultaneously-valid links live for up to an hour. An old email sitting in an inbox, a mail relay log, or a shared/compromised mailbox remains a valid credential-reset vector even after the user believes they've completed the flow with a later link.

findings_initial.title: A successful password reset does not revoke other outstanding tokens for the same account
findings_initial.requirement: OWASP Forgot Password / Session Management guidance: once a reset token is redeemed, all other live reset tokens for that account should be invalidated, since they represent parallel, unaccounted-for paths to change the credential.
findings_initial.evidence: app/auth.py:111-128 — reset_password() deletes only the single token key that was redeemed (line 127); it never scans/purges other entries in self._tokens whose stored email matches the same user.
findings_initial.failure: If two reset emails were sent (e.g., user retried, or an attacker triggered a reset to phish/intercept a link) and the legitimate user redeems one, the other token remains valid until its own expiry, giving an attacker who obtained the second link a window to reset the password again after the legitimate user thinks the account is secured.

findings_initial.title: No confirmation/notification email is sent after a password reset succeeds
findings_initial.requirement: OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet: 'Notify the user of password change' — a separate email confirming the credential was changed must be sent so the legitimate owner can detect and react to an unauthorized reset.
findings_initial.evidence: app/auth.py:111-128 — reset_password() updates user.password_hash and returns True, but calls self.mailer.send(...) nowhere in this method; only request_reset() ever emails the user.
findings_initial.failure: If an attacker who intercepted or guessed a valid token resets the password, the real account owner receives no signal that their credential changed, delaying detection of account takeover.

findings_initial.title: Expired reset tokens are only removed when someone attempts to redeem them, so unredeemed tokens are never cleaned up
findings_initial.requirement: Lifecycle/resource-management expectation for any TTL-based token store used by a long-running service: expired entries must not accumulate unboundedly in memory just because no one happened to look them up.
findings_initial.evidence: app/auth.py:117-119 and :113 — the only code paths that call `del self._tokens[token]` are inside reset_password(), which only runs for a token someone actually submits. request_reset() never sweeps or bounds self._tokens, and there is no background/periodic purge.
findings_initial.failure: In production, every forgot-password request that is never completed (user ignores the email, link expires unclicked) leaves a permanent dict entry. Over the service's lifetime this is unbounded memory growth, and is trivially acceleratable by anyone repeatedly POSTing known/guessed emails to request_reset(), turning it into a low-cost memory-exhaustion vector against a long-lived process.

findings_final.title: Reset tokens live only in a per-instance Python dict
findings_final.requirement: A password-reset link must remain valid for its full TTL regardless of which process or server handles the follow-up request — an implicit lifecycle requirement of any multi-request flow (request happens on one HTTP call, redemption on a later, possibly different, call).
findings_final.evidence: app/auth.py:92 — `self._tokens: dict[str, tuple[str, float]] = {}` is instance state with no backing store (file, cache, DB). `PasswordResetService` is constructed fresh per call site with no shared persistence layer.
findings_final.failure: In any production deployment with more than one worker process/thread pool, container replica, or a deploy/restart between the two clicks, the token minted in request_reset on instance A will not exist on instance B (or after a restart) when reset_password is called. Legitimate users clicking a valid, unexpired link get 'invalid token' and the four-a-week support burden this ticket was meant to eliminate returns.

findings_final.title: reset_password accepts any new_password, including empty string
findings_final.requirement: A password-reset endpoint must enforce the same minimum password policy as account creation (NIST SP 800-63B minimum length / OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet) — a reset must not be a backdoor around registration-time password rules.
findings_final.evidence: app/auth.py:134-147 — `reset_password` calls `hash_password(new_password)` unconditionally; there is no length, emptiness, or complexity check anywhere in the method.
findings_final.failure: A user (or an attacker who obtained a token via a shared device or leaked email) can set the account password to `''` or `'a'`, silently downgrading account security below whatever bar registration enforces, and support has no record of it happening.

findings_final.title: Full reset token is kept in memory as the dict key, not a hash of it
findings_final.requirement: OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet: the reset token, like a password, should be stored server-side as a hash, so possession of the server's memory/log/dump does not itself grant the ability to redeem outstanding tokens.
findings_final.evidence: app/auth.py:113-119 — `token = new_token()` ... `self._tokens[token] = (email, expires_at)` stores the raw, usable token verbatim as the dictionary key.
findings_final.failure: Any process-memory disclosure, core dump, or accidental debug log of `self._tokens` hands an attacker live, redeemable reset tokens for every user with an outstanding request, equivalent to leaking their new-password credentials directly.

findings_final.title: request_reset has no throttling per email or per caller
findings_final.requirement: OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet requires rate-limiting / lockout on the reset-request endpoint to prevent abuse (mail-bombing a victim's inbox, resource exhaustion).
findings_final.evidence: app/auth.py:107-132 — `request_reset` performs `self.mailer.send(...)` on every single call with no counter, cooldown, or per-address cap.
findings_final.failure: An attacker can call `request_reset('victim@example.com')` in a tight loop to flood the victim's inbox with reset emails (harassment / mail-bombing), or hammer the mailer/backing SMTP service to exhaust it, with no defense in this layer.

findings_final.title: self._tokens is mutated without any concurrency control
findings_final.requirement: A service invoked from a multi-threaded/multi-request web server must keep shared mutable state consistent under concurrent calls (basic thread-safety expectation for 'two attempts at once').
findings_final.evidence: app/auth.py:94-105 — `_prune_expired` and `_invalidate_tokens_for` each build a list of keys then `del self._tokens[t]` in a second pass, with no lock; `request_reset`/`reset_password` read-then-write `self._tokens` and `user.password_hash` with no synchronization.
findings_final.failure: Two concurrent calls (e.g. two in-flight requests for the same email, or a client retry racing the original request) can both pass the expiry/removal check for the same key and the second `del self._tokens[t]` raises `KeyError`, crashing the request; concurrent redemption/invalidation can also race and leave inconsistent state.

findings_final.title: Email is looked up in the user store with exact-string matching
findings_final.requirement: Standard practice for account-lookup email handling (and most mail providers' actual case-insensitive treatment of the local-part) is to normalize email addresses before comparison, so a user who types their address in a different case can still find their account.
findings_final.evidence: app/auth.py:115 — `user = self.users.get(email)` does a raw dict lookup with no case-folding or trimming of the input email.
findings_final.failure: A user who signed up as 'Ada@Example.com' but types 'ada@example.com' (or vice versa) when requesting a reset silently gets the generic 'if an account exists' email and no actual reset link, reintroducing the support burden this feature was built to remove.

findings_initial.title: A processor failure (5xx) is cached permanently against the idempotency key, blocking all future legitimate retries
findings_initial.requirement: Idempotency-key semantics (Stripe's documented contract, which this design mirrors): only the definitive outcome of a completed attempt should be memoized so that a client can safely retry after a transient/ambiguous failure and eventually get a real result. An error caused by the processor itself must not permanently lock the key to that error.
findings_initial.evidence: app/charges.py post_charge: `status, body = self._execute(params)` followed unconditionally by `self._idempotency_cache[idempotency_key] = (status, body)` -- this runs the same way whether `_execute` returned 200 or the simulated 500 'processor unavailable'. Any subsequent call with the same key hits the cache-hit branch at the top of `post_charge` and returns the stale 500 without ever calling `_execute` again.
findings_initial.failure: This is exactly the scenario PAY-208 exists to fix: the mobile SDK retries automatically with the same key after a dropped/failed request. If the first attempt failed with a transient processor error, every automatic retry now returns the cached 500 forever -- the charge can never succeed with that key. The customer's checkout is permanently stuck, support reopens the same class of ticket, and the likely 'fix' (mint a new idempotency key on error and retry) reintroduces the double-charge risk this feature is supposed to eliminate, since the original 500 may have been an ambiguous outcome where the processor actually moved money.

findings_initial.title: Two simultaneous requests with the same idempotency key both pass the cache-miss check and both execute the charge
findings_initial.requirement: Idempotency-key contract for concurrent duplicate requests: a second request arriving with a key that is already in flight must not be allowed to independently execute the side effect -- it must either wait/lock or be rejected (e.g. HTTP 409 'a request with this idempotency key is already in progress'), never race to a second `_execute`.
findings_initial.evidence: app/charges.py post_charge implements a check-then-act sequence with no lock: `if idempotency_key ... in self._idempotency_cache: return ...` then later `self._idempotency_cache[idempotency_key] = (status, body)`. Nothing marks the key as 'in progress' between the cache check and the cache write, and `_execute` (and `before_execute`, which Operations explicitly monkey-patches to inject latency) sits in between with no synchronization.
findings_initial.failure: The ticket's own root cause is a dropped connection triggering a client retry while the original request may still be in flight upstream. If the retry races the original before the first `_execute` call returns and writes the cache entry, both calls see a cache miss, both call `_execute`, and the customer is charged twice -- the exact double-charge bug this feature was built to close, now happening through the idempotency path itself instead of around it.

findings_initial.title: Reusing a key with a different request body silently returns the stale cached charge instead of rejecting the mismatch
findings_initial.requirement: Standard idempotency-key semantics (as documented by Stripe and other processors this pattern imitates): a key must be scoped to one specific request payload. Replaying the same key with different parameters (different amount, currency, etc.) must return an error, not the cached result for the original, different request.
findings_initial.evidence: app/charges.py post_charge only keys the cache on `idempotency_key` and never compares the incoming `params` against the params that produced the cached entry: `if idempotency_key is not None and idempotency_key in self._idempotency_cache: return self._idempotency_cache[idempotency_key]`.
findings_initial.failure: A client bug or key-collision (e.g. a poorly-generated key, or a UI that reuses a key across a corrected order) causes a request for one amount to silently receive a 200 confirming a charge for a different amount that was never actually made for the new params. The caller believes a $X charge succeeded when only the original $Y charge exists on the ledger -- a billing-integrity defect a payments reviewer would block on.

findings_initial.title: Idempotency keys and their cached responses live forever with no TTL, unlike the standard window this pattern is modeled on
findings_initial.requirement: Idempotency-key lifecycle convention (e.g. Stripe expires keys after 24 hours): keys must expire after a bounded window so storage doesn't grow without bound and so the same key value can legitimately be reused for a new operation after the window passes.
findings_initial.evidence: app/charges.py: `self._idempotency_cache: dict[str, tuple[int, dict]] = {}` is written to in `post_charge` and never pruned or checked against `self.clock.now()`. The injected `Clock` (with its `advance()` method, clearly provided for exercising time-based expiry) is never consulted anywhere in `post_charge`.
findings_initial.failure: In production the cache grows unbounded for the lifetime of the process, and a key can never be reused even long after the original transaction context is irrelevant, contradicting how every real idempotency-key implementation this feature is modeled on actually behaves. This also means capacity/memory planning for the service is impossible to reason about.

findings_final.title: An exception during _execute()/before_execute() permanently strands the key in 'in_progress', blocking every legitimate retry for 24h
findings_final.requirement: The ticket's own stated goal: 'the client's connection drops, it retries the charge... if we see the same key again we shouldn't put a second charge through' implies a retry after a failed/interrupted attempt must eventually be able to complete. The claim-then-execute-then-release logic in post_charge has no try/finally, so any exception between the claim (line 129) and the cache update (line 145) leaves the entry as status='in_progress' forever, with nothing to release it short of the 24h TTL.
findings_final.evidence: app/charges.py post_charge: the block from 'self._idempotency_cache[idempotency_key] = {...status: in_progress...}' through '_execute(params)' and the final cache update has no exception handling. Reproduced: monkey-patching before_execute to raise ConnectionError (simulating exactly the 'processor call fails/connection drops' scenario Operations is documented to inject via before_execute) leaves the cache entry stuck at status='in_progress'; a subsequent retry with the corrected/working call gets HTTP 409 'already in progress' instead of completing, and api.executed stays empty.
findings_final.failure: The exact scenario PAY-208 was filed to fix -- a dropped connection followed by a client retry -- now results in the customer's charge never going through at all for up to 24 hours, instead of a double charge. This trades double-charge tickets for 'my payment is stuck/rejected' tickets, which for a P1 payments endpoint is arguably worse since the merchant now believes the charge failed and may abandon checkout.

findings_final.title: _prune_expired deletes idempotency entries by age alone, including ones still status='in_progress', letting a concurrent/late retry bypass the in-progress guard and execute a second real charge
findings_final.requirement: Idempotency-key semantics (mirrored from Stripe, per the code's own comment) require that a key which is currently being processed cannot be reused to trigger a second attempt -- 'two attempts at once' must collapse to one execution regardless of elapsed time. An in-flight claim must never lapse purely due to TTL; only completed (done) entries should expire.
findings_final.evidence: app/charges.py:97-103 _entry_expired/_prune_expired check only entry['created_at'] and the fixed TTL, never entry['status']. Reproduced: seeding the cache with a status='in_progress' entry, advancing the injected Clock past the 24h TTL, then calling post_charge with the same key causes _prune_expired to delete the stale-but-still-in-flight claim, after which the request is treated as brand new and executed for real (HTTP 200, a genuine _execute call) instead of returning 409.
findings_final.failure: If an original attempt is slow, hung, or (combined with the missing try/finally above) permanently stuck 'in_progress', any retry that arrives after the 24h window silently executes a second real charge against the processor instead of being deduplicated -- the double-charge bug the ticket exists to prevent, just delayed by up to a day.

findings_final.title: Cached idempotency entries store the caller's params dict by reference, not a copy, so post-call mutation of that dict defeats the 'same key, different params → reject' check
findings_final.requirement: Idempotency-key contract requires that reusing a key with materially different request parameters be rejected (the code implements this via entry['params'] != params at line 120), which implicitly requires the recorded params to be an immutable snapshot of what was actually charged.
findings_final.evidence: app/charges.py stores '"params": params' directly (lines 131 and 151) instead of a copy such as dict(params). Reproduced: calling post_charge(params, key='k1'), then mutating params['amount'] in place before calling post_charge(params, key='k1') again causes the second call to be treated as identical (no 409), returning the cached first response -- silently masking that the second call actually requested a different amount.
findings_final.failure: Any caller pattern that reuses/mutates the same dict object across a retry (common with retry helpers, middleware that annotates the body, or connection-pooled request objects) can cause a request for a different amount to silently return a stale cached response instead of being rejected, corrupting what the ledger/response tells the client actually happened.

findings_final.title: The idempotency cache and lock are in-memory and process-local, so retries routed to a different instance (or after a restart) are not deduplicated at all
findings_final.requirement: A production idempotency-key implementation for a horizontally scaled payments service must make the dedup state visible to whichever instance handles the retry -- otherwise the guarantee only holds by accident of load-balancer stickiness.
findings_final.evidence: app/charges.py:__init__ defines self._idempotency_cache and self._lock as plain in-process dict/threading.Lock with no persistence or shared-store backing; there is no mechanism for a second ChargeAPI instance (a second process/pod) to see a claim made by another.
findings_final.failure: In any real deployment with more than one process (which is the norm for a payments endpoint under a P1 double-charge incident), a dropped-connection retry that lands on a different instance -- or any retry after the original process restarts/redeploys -- bypasses the idempotency check entirely and re-executes the charge, reproducing the exact double-charge incidents PAY-208 was filed to close.

findings_final.title: idempotency_key accepts any string of any length/content with no size or format limit
findings_final.requirement: Published idempotency-key implementations (e.g. Stripe's, referenced in this file's own TTL comment) bound the key to a reasonable length (Stripe: max 255 characters) precisely because the key is used as an unbounded-lifetime cache key.
findings_final.evidence: app/charges.py post_charge only checks 'idempotency_key is None'; there is no length or character-set validation before using it as a dict key that persists in _idempotency_cache for up to 24 hours.
findings_final.failure: A malicious or buggy client can send arbitrarily large keys (megabytes each) repeatedly, growing the in-memory cache unbounded until the TTL sweep catches up, a low-cost memory-exhaustion vector against a payments endpoint.

findings_initial.title: A single oversized field raises an uncaught exception and aborts the entire import
findings_initial.requirement: Ticket contract: 'A row that cannot be imported goes in errors... A file with unimportable rows still imports the rows that are fine.' Any single bad row must degrade to a reported error, not fail the whole request.
findings_initial.evidence: app/importer.py:58 iterates `for line_number, row in enumerate(reader, ...)` with no try/except around the loop. Python's csv module enforces a field size limit (128KB) and raises `_csv.Error: field larger than field limit` when exceeded. Reproduced: a single field of ~200KB (e.g. a corrupted export or a pasted blob in one cell) causes `import_users` to raise instead of returning an ImportResult.
findings_initial.failure: One malformed/oversized row in an otherwise-valid 340-row HR export causes the whole upload to 500 instead of importing the 339 good rows and reporting one error, exactly the failure mode the ticket says must not happen. Since customer-produced files are explicitly uncontrolled input, this is a realistic and easily-triggered case, not a hypothetical.

findings_initial.title: Required-column check is case-sensitive, so a differently-cased header rejects the entire file
findings_initial.requirement: Ticket: 'email, name and team must be present' — from customer-supplied HR exports/spreadsheets whose header casing is not controlled by us ('the files come from the customer's own systems... we don't control how they're produced').
findings_initial.evidence: app/importer.py:51 does `column not in header` as an exact string match after only `.strip()`. Reproduced: header `Email,Name,Team` (capitalized, as many HR/spreadsheet exports produce) is reported as missing all three required columns and the whole file is rejected with zero rows imported.
findings_initial.failure: A perfectly valid file from a customer whose export tool capitalizes headers is rejected outright with a confusing 'missing required columns' error, even though the required data is present — this is exactly the class of file the feature was built to accept.

findings_initial.title: Duplicate email rows within one file are silently imported as separate users
findings_initial.requirement: Implicit requirement of a user-import feature: email is the identity key for a user account, so two rows with the same email (including case-insensitive dupes) must not silently produce two accounts or two conflicting records.
findings_initial.evidence: app/importer.py has no dedup/uniqueness check across `result.users`. Reproduced: a file with `ada@example.com` appearing twice with different names/teams produces two entries in `result.users`, no error.
findings_initial.failure: HR exports commonly contain duplicate rows (e.g. a user listed under two teams, or a re-exported row). Downstream user-creation will either error confusingly per-row, silently overwrite one record with another, or create duplicate accounts — and the admin gets no warning from the importer that this happened.

findings_initial.title: A repeated column name in the header silently overwrites earlier values with no error
findings_initial.requirement: Ticket: 'Rows that can't be imported get reported back to the admin' — data loss from an ambiguous header should be surfaced, not silently swallowed.
findings_initial.evidence: app/importer.py:69 builds the record with `{name: value for name, value in zip(header, row)}`. Reproduced: header `email,name,team,email` with a row `a@example.com,Ada,Eng,other@example.com` produces `email: 'other@example.com'`, silently discarding the first email column's value with no error or warning.
findings_initial.failure: A malformed or accidentally duplicated export column (easy to produce from a spreadsheet with a stray copy-pasted column) causes one of the user's real field values to vanish without any indication to the admin that data was dropped.

findings_initial.title: Reported row numbers do not match physical file lines when a field contains an embedded newline
findings_initial.requirement: RFC 4180 permits quoted fields to contain embedded newlines; the ticket implies errors are 'reported back to the admin' so they can find and fix the offending row in their source file.
findings_initial.evidence: app/importer.py:58 uses `enumerate(reader, start=2)`, which counts logical CSV records, not physical text lines. Reproduced: a file where row 2 contains a quoted multi-line name causes the next data row (physical line 4) to be reported as 'Row 3', an off-by-one (or more, depending on how many embedded newlines preceded it) mismatch against the actual file.
findings_initial.failure: An admin trying to locate 'Row 3' in a text editor or spreadsheet to fix the reported error will look at the wrong line, especially in larger files with several multi-line fields, making the error report actively misleading rather than merely imprecise.

findings_initial.title: Field values are stored verbatim, including spreadsheet-formula payloads
findings_initial.requirement: OWASP CSV Injection guidance: untrusted CSV cell values beginning with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@` (or tab/CR) must be neutralized before the data is later rendered or re-exported into a spreadsheet, since the source file is explicitly untrusted customer input.
findings_initial.evidence: app/importer.py:69 only applies `.strip()` to each cell; no check or escaping for formula-trigger characters is performed before values land in `result.users`.
findings_initial.failure: If the admin UI or any downstream tooling later exports the imported user list back to CSV/Excel (a common admin convenience action), a name/team field crafted as `=HYPERLINK(...)` or `=cmd|'/c calc'!A1` from a compromised or malicious customer export can execute on the admin's machine when opened.

findings_final.title: CSV-injection mitigation mutates the stored email/name/team values themselves, not just a display copy
findings_final.requirement: The imported record's email must be the literal, correct account identifier the customer supplied (contract: `result.users` feeds account provisioning/login, not a spreadsheet render). The OWASP CSV-injection mitigation (prefixing =,+,-,@ with an apostrophe) is meant to be applied when *rendering/exporting* data back into a spreadsheet, not when ingesting the source-of-truth value.
findings_final.evidence: app/importer.py:103-106,138-146 — `_sanitize_cell` is applied to every cell before validation/storage. Any email, name, or team starting with '=', '+', '-', or '@' gets a literal apostrophe prepended and that mutated string is what ends up in `result.users`. Verified: `+alerts@example.com` is stored as `'+alerts@example.com`; `@example.com` is stored as `'@example.com`; a team named `-Ops` is stored as `'-Ops`.
findings_final.failure: Any legitimate email using plus-addressing, or any name/team beginning with a hyphen (common in HR exports, e.g. '-TEMP', '-Contractor'), silently gets a corrupted value baked into the account record with no error reported. The admin sees a clean import with zero errors, but the created account's email no longer matches what the customer's HR system has, breaking SSO/login and any downstream email delivery to that user.

findings_final.title: Classic Mac / lone-CR line endings crash the whole upload instead of being reported as an error
findings_final.requirement: Ticket: "Rows that can't be imported get reported back to the admin, and the rest of the file still imports" and "we don't control how [files] are produced." A parser accepting arbitrary customer-produced files must not raise an unhandled exception for a file it cannot parse.
findings_final.evidence: app/importer.py:44-48 — the header line is read via `next(reader)` guarded only by `except StopIteration`, with no `except csv.Error`. A file using bare `\r` line endings (old Mac exports, some legacy HR/mainframe tooling) causes `io.StringIO` to yield the whole file as one line, and `csv.reader` raises `_csv.Error: new-line character seen in unquoted field` on the very first `next(reader)` call. Reproduced directly: `import_users('email,name,team\rada@example.com,...\r')` raises uncaught.
findings_final.failure: The admin upload endpoint gets an unhandled exception (likely a 500) instead of a clean 'file could not be read' or per-row error result, for a file format variant that is squarely within the stated 'whatever they've got' scope. The 340-user onboarding this ticket exists to speed up fails outright with no diagnostic message.

findings_final.title: Email validation only checks for the presence of '@', accepting structurally invalid addresses
findings_final.requirement: Ticket: rows that can't be imported must be reported as errors, not silently added to `result.users`. An address that is not a deliverable email is a row that 'can't be imported' for a feature whose entire purpose is provisioning login/notification accounts.
findings_final.evidence: app/importer.py:111 — validation is `elif "@" not in record["email"]`. Verified `ada@` (no domain), `@example.com` (no local part), and `a@b@c` (multiple '@') all pass validation and land in `result.users` with zero errors.
findings_final.failure: Malformed addresses from messy HR exports are silently provisioned as real user accounts instead of being flagged for the admin to fix, producing accounts that can never receive an invite/notification email and that the admin has no indication need correcting.

findings_final.title: Semicolon-delimited exports (common from EU-locale Excel) are rejected with a misleading 'missing column' error
findings_final.requirement: Ticket: "The files come from the customer's own systems ... whatever they've got — so we don't control how they're produced." No delimiter detection is attempted, and the resulting error misrepresents the actual problem.
findings_final.evidence: app/importer.py:43 — `csv.reader` is constructed with default comma delimiter and no `csv.Sniffer`/dialect detection. A semicolon-delimited file with all three required columns present produces `errors: ['Missing required column(s): email, name, team']`, which is factually wrong (the columns are present, just not comma-separated).
findings_final.failure: Admins receive a confusing error that says required columns are missing when the file actually has them, for a very common real-world export variant (Excel in most European locales defaults CSV export to semicolons because comma is the decimal separator), wasting support time diagnosing a self-inflicted red herring.
